newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean navy ships again confront N.Korean boat.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean navy ships again confront N.Korean boat.

text.p: South Korean navy vessels confronted a North Korean patrol boat for a second day on Friday without any incident, a Seoul military spokesman said.
He said a North Korean navy boat entered South Korean waters as it was trying to stop a Chinese fishing boat operating in northern waters.
"It was the second such intrusion in two days and the fifth this year," the spokesman said. "I believe none of the North Korean vessels involved had any intention to provoke our side."
Five South Korean navy vessels confronted the North Korean patrol boat for less than two hours before it headed north.
On Thursday, North Korean patrol boats were confronted after entering southern waters to stop a Chinese fishing boat heading south in the Yellow Sea.
Tension has always been high along the Korean border since the 1950-53 Korean War ended in a truce rather than a peace treaty.
On Wednesday, a South Korean man fishing at night on a small boat was shot dead by southern soldiers who mistook him as a North Korean infiltrator, a defence ministry official said.
The man was among six people fishing off South Korea's southern city of Pusan in an area declared off-limits for civilians.

"They ignored orders to stop and began fleeing. Soldiers guarding the coast mistook them for North Korean spies and opened fire on them," the official said. The five others were captured but released after being warned.
South Korea has been closely guarding its coastlines since a North Korean submarine landed 26 commandos in the south last September.
In December, Pyongyang apologised for the incident after 24 of the commandos were shot dead during a two-month manhunt by southern troops. One was captured and the other is still at large.
Meanwhile, South Korea's Unification Ministry spokesman Kang Ho-yang on Friday urged the North to seek detente with the South and open an "era of reconciliation and cooperation".

"The North should cooperate to consolidate peace in the Korean peninsula by successfully holding four-party talks in the near future," Kang said in a statement marking the 25th anniversary of a joint communique issued by the two Koreas.

The 1972 communique, in which the rival states pledged efforts to build mutual trust and expand exchanges, was issued simultaneously in Seoul and Pyongyang after a secret exchange of visits by presidential envoys.
Despite the communique, the two Koreas soon resumed hostility and the Korean border remains one of the world's last Cold War frontiers.
The North has agreed to a meeting on August 5 in New York of senior officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China to arrange four-nation peace talks.
The four-nation talks are aimed at working out a permanent peace settlement to replace the fraying 1953 ceasefire pact.
